parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A man calls a language school to ask about evening Japanese classes.
script: Good evening, Westfield Language School. How can I help?
Hi. I'm interested in your Japanese classes for adults. I'm going to Japan for work next year.
Lovely. Have you studied Japanese before?
A little, using an app. I can read hiragana but not much else.
Then you'd probably start in our Elementary class rather than complete Beginners. Elementary meets on Tuesday evenings.
From 6.45 to 8.45. The course runs for twelve weeks, starting on the 13th of January.
The full fee is 240 pounds, but if you book before the end of this month, there's an early booking discount, which brings it down to 210.
I'll book now, then. Is the textbook extra?
Yes, it's 18 pounds, and you buy it from us at the first lesson. We also recommend a good dictionary app, but that's optional.
Ms Fujimoto. She's been teaching here for eight years. F-U-J-I-M-O-T-O.
Great. And where is the class held? At the main building?
Not this term. The main building is being repaired, so Japanese classes are in our annexe on Bridge Street, room 4, on the second floor.
There's no parking at the annexe, I'm afraid, but the bus stop is right outside, and the multi-storey car park on Mill Road is a five-minute walk.
That's fine. Can I take a test to check my level?
Yes, there's a short online placement test. I'll email you the link. Could I take your email address?
It's omar.haddad at mailbox dot com. Haddad is H-A-D-D-A-D.
Thank you. You'll get the link today.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: A ranger talks to visitors at the start of a guided walk in a nature reserve.
script: Morning, everyone, and welcome to Fernhill Nature Reserve. I'm Josh, one of the rangers, and I'll be leading today's walk. Before we set off, a few points.

The reserve covers about four hundred hectares. It used to be farmland, and most of it was drained for cattle. Twenty years ago the trust bought the land and allowed the wetlands to return, which is why we now have so many birds.
Today's walk is about five kilometres and should take around two and a half hours, with a stop at the bird hide. The path can be muddy near the lake, so I'm glad to see most of you in boots.
Please keep dogs on a lead at all times. That's not because of other visitors, but because ground-nesting birds are very easily disturbed at this time of year.
You'll notice there are no rubbish bins on the reserve. That's deliberate: bins attract foxes and crows, which take eggs. So please take everything home with you.

If you'd like to come back, the visitor centre runs a volunteer day on the first Sunday of every month. At the moment we especially need help with clearing young trees from the heathland, which would otherwise turn into woodland.

Now let me show you the route on this map. We're standing at the car park, at the southern edge of the reserve. We'll head north along the main track. After about a kilometre you'll see the old barn on your left; it's now used to store equipment, so it's closed to the public.
Just beyond the barn, the track splits. We'll take the right-hand path down to the lake. The bird hide is on the east shore of the lake, and that's where we'll stop for a break.

From the hide we'll walk round the north end of the lake to the viewpoint on top of Fern Hill, which is the highest point of the reserve. Then we come back down through the woods on the west side, past the pond where children can go pond-dipping in summer, and back to the car park. The visitor centre, with the café, is right next to the car park.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: Two business students, Lena and Kwame, talk about a work placement report.
script: Hi Kwame. Have you started your placement report yet?
Only the introduction. My placement at the logistics firm was great, but I'm finding it hard to write about.
Same. What did you enjoy most?
Honestly, it was being trusted with a real project. I had to redesign the way they record returned parcels. I expected to be making coffee and filing, but they gave me responsibility from week two.

Lucky you. In my marketing placement, the most useful thing was actually watching how my manager dealt with clients. She was so calm on the phone, even when clients were angry. I learned more from that than from any project.
The hours. I was commuting ninety minutes each way, so I was exhausted by Friday. The work itself was fine.
For me it was the software. Their system was really old and nobody had written down how it worked.
Now, the report guidelines say we should include a section on what we'd do differently. Any ideas?
I'd ask for feedback more often. I only had one review, at the end, and some of the comments would have been useful earlier.
Good point. I think I'd keep a daily diary. When I started writing the report, I'd forgotten half of what I did in the first month.
Let's look at the marking criteria. What do you think gets the most marks?
The tutor said reflection is worth the most: forty per cent. Description of the organisation is only fifteen.
Ten per cent. The rest is the analysis of a problem in the workplace, thirty-five per cent.
So reflection matters most. Shall we read each other's drafts next week?
Yes, but let's swap on Thursday, not Monday. I've got an exam on Monday.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecture on the history of the shipping container.
script: Today we're looking at an invention that changed the world economy, even though most people never think about it: the shipping container.

Before the 1950s, cargo was loaded onto ships piece by piece: sacks, barrels and wooden crates, each one carried by hand. This method was called break-bulk shipping. It was slow, and a ship could spend a week in port being loaded and unloaded. It was also expensive, because huge numbers of dock workers were needed, and theft was common.

The man usually credited with the container is Malcom McLean, who owned a trucking company in the United States. In 1956 he converted an old tanker ship to carry fifty-eight metal boxes, which could be lifted straight from a truck onto the ship by crane. The cost of loading fell by more than ninety per cent.

However, the real breakthrough came in the late 1960s, when the size of containers was standardised. Before that, every company used boxes of different sizes, so a container from one firm could not be handled at another firm's port. Standard sizes, together with standard corner fittings, meant that any container could be moved by any crane, truck or train, anywhere in the world.

The effects were enormous. Ports had to be rebuilt, often in new locations with deep water and space for storage, so many old city-centre docks closed. In London, for example, the old docks were later redeveloped as offices and housing. The number of dock workers fell sharply.
For manufacturers, cheap transport made it possible to produce goods far from where they were sold. Many economists argue that the container did more to increase world trade than any trade agreement.

Today, the largest ships can carry over twenty thousand containers. But there are new challenges. Thousands of containers are lost at sea every year, mainly during storms, and shipping produces around three per cent of global carbon emissions. Some companies are now testing ships powered by ammonia, which produces no carbon when burned.

passages.title: Greenleaf Supermarkets: guidance for new checkout staff
paras: Starting your shift. Arrive ten minutes before your shift begins, so that you can collect your till drawer from the cash office and count the float. Any difference must be reported before you open your till.

Age-restricted products. Customers buying alcohol, knives or certain medicines must be asked for ID if they look under 25. Accepted ID is a passport, a photo driving licence or a national ID card. If in doubt, call a supervisor.
Refunds. Checkout staff cannot give refunds. Customers wanting to return an item should be sent to the customer service desk near the entrance.
Breaks. On shifts of more than six hours you are entitled to a 30-minute unpaid break and two 10-minute paid breaks. Breaks are arranged by the shift supervisor.
Uniform. Your uniform and name badge are provided. Staff must wear plain black trousers or a skirt and closed shoes, which are not provided.
Discounts. After four weeks' employment, you will receive a staff card giving 10% off most purchases.

passages.title: How to make a good impression in your first job
paras: A  Punctuality matters more than many young workers realise. Arriving a few minutes early shows that you take the job seriously, and if you are ever going to be late, phone your manager before your shift starts rather than sending a message afterwards.
B  You will not know everything in your first few weeks, and nobody expects you to. It is far better to ask a colleague how something is done than to guess and make a costly mistake.
C  Try to learn the names of the people you work with as quickly as possible. A simple technique is to write them down, with a short note about each person's role, at the end of your first day.
D  Your manager may give you feedback that is hard to hear. Listen without arguing, thank them, and ask what you could do differently. Managers notice who responds well to criticism.
E  Social media can damage a career. Never post complaints about your employer, customers or colleagues online, even on a private account. Screenshots are easily shared.
F  Finally, look after yourself. A new job can be tiring, so make sure you get enough sleep and keep some time for friends and interests outside work.

passages.title: The four-day working week
paras: A  The idea that people could work fewer hours for the same pay is not new. In 1930 the economist John Maynard Keynes predicted that, thanks to rising productivity, his grandchildren would work only fifteen hours a week. That has not happened. In most rich countries, full-time employees still work around forty hours, much as they did in the 1950s.

B  In recent years, however, interest in a shorter week has grown sharply. The largest trial so far took place in the United Kingdom in 2022, when around sixty companies, ranging from banks to fish-and-chip shops, agreed to reduce staff hours by twenty per cent for six months without cutting pay. In return, employees were expected to maintain their usual output.

C  The results were striking. Most companies reported that productivity stayed the same or improved, and around nine out of ten decided to continue with the shorter week after the trial ended. Staff reported less stress and better sleep, and the number of sick days fell by about two thirds. Recruitment also became easier: several firms said the four-day week attracted applicants who would otherwise have gone to competitors offering higher salaries.

D  How can people do the same work in less time? Researchers point to several factors. Meetings were shortened or cut altogether, and many companies introduced periods of the day when staff were not to be interrupted by email or messages. Some employees admitted that, in a five-day week, a surprising amount of time had been spent on tasks that added little value.

E  Not everyone is convinced. Critics note that the companies in the trial chose to take part, so they may have been unusually well suited to the change. Organisations that must provide a service every day, such as hospitals, schools and shops, cannot simply close on Fridays, and would need to employ more staff to cover the missing hours. Economist Rachel Turner also warns that the benefits may fade: 'When the novelty wears off, old habits can return.'

F  Some countries are now experimenting at a national level. Iceland ran public-sector trials between 2015 and 2019 that led to most workers gaining the right to shorter hours, and several governments in Europe have funded trials of their own. Whether the four-day week becomes normal will probably depend less on evidence than on whether employers believe it gives them an advantage in competing for skilled workers.
